rows.body: This tab helps owners and investors understand typical economics and obligations for this brand before detailed modeling. It describes patterns—not quotes, property-level forecasts, or a substitute for the franchise disclosure document, LOI, or your advisors.

Affiliation with this brand usually means trading a recurring fee stack and program participation for enterprise distribution, loyalty access, operating systems, and brand-led demand support. Owners still fund conversion or new-build standards, working capital through ramp, and periodic capital for brand compliance—while negotiating which items are fixed versus deal-dependent.

rows.title: Royalty / brand fee
rows.body: Ongoing compensation for brand standards, QA, and system access. Basis and timing are defined in disclosure documents; conversion and market tier often influence how the fee is framed in the LOI.

rows.title: Marketing / brand fund
rows.body: Supports portfolio campaigns, digital presence, and sales tools. Owners evaluate net contribution after assessing how much demand is brand-driven versus property-led.

rows.title: Technology / systems
rows.body: Mandatory stack participation (PMS, CRS, and related interfaces) is typical. Owners should plan implementation, training, and interface costs beyond the recurring tech line item.

rows.title: Loyalty / program participation
rows.body: Program enrollment links the property to member recognition and direct-channel mechanics. Owners should understand chargeback themes and reporting obligations in diligence—not just the headline fee category.

rows.title: Reservation / distribution
rows.body: Covers brand-mediated booking paths and related services. Evaluate alongside OTA mix and loyalty contribution in the operating pro forma.

rows.title: Training / opening support
rows.body: Pre-opening and opening assistance, certifications, and onboarding. Often weighted toward the opening window rather than steady state.

Room count, market tier, airport versus resort positioning, conversion scope, incentive package, and whether a third-party operator leads opening usually change which fees apply and how capital is phased.

Brands in this tier often discuss key money, marketing support, fee ramps, or conversion assistance in competitive situations. Structure, timing, and clawback are deal-specific—confirm what was actually offered for your asset, not what is typical in marketing materials.

Typical conversion or new-build path:

Application and feasibility alignment with brand development

Design and standards review (kit-of-parts where applicable)

Pre-opening planning: staffing plans, OS&E alignment, systems implementation

Brand-led opening support: training, QA readiness, soft opening coordination

Stabilization period with heightened brand touchpoints and reporting

Owners with a third-party operator often run opening through the operator while the brand approves milestones.

Financial planning themes (no deal-specific amounts on this page):

Front-loaded spend for standards compliance, FF&E, and technology cutover

Working capital held through ramp while mix and rate build

Fee stack that may step from opening/training-weighted to stabilized recurring charges

Potential incentive credits or ramps that change early-year cash burden

Reserve and PIP expectations documented for renewal—even if opening PIP is lighter

Model should separate owner-funded capex, brand/program fees, and operator pass-throughs.

Expect a long initial franchise term with renewal options subject to notice, conditions, and brand standards compliance. Renewal may trigger property improvement expectations; confirm duration, notice party, and conditions in the agreement—not on this overview.

Performance tests and QA programs are common themes—understand cure periods and who may terminate after failure.

Early exit without cause may be limited; termination fees or liquidated damages may apply depending on structure.

Audit rights and caps on reimbursable expenses are worth confirming with counsel.

rows.title: Area of protection
rows.body: Radius and restriction themes define how the brand limits same-brand competition near your site—confirm exact geography in legal documents.

rows.title: Transfer & sale
rows.body: Assignment, change-of-control, and buyout provisions affect liquidity. Plan for brand approval paths before assuming a sale is frictionless.

rows.title: LOI & process
rows.body: Timeline from LOI to definitive agreement varies; understand which LOI terms tend to be binding versus exploratory.

Beyond fees: mandatory systems, reporting cadence, training cycles, and brand program participation require owner and operator time. Communication expectations and dispute paths should be understood before signing.

Owner typically funds: Front-loaded standards and FF&E alignment, technology cutover, working capital through opening, and application or training cash outlays.

Brand typically provides: Design and standards review, opening playbooks, pre-opening support, and milestone QA—not day-to-day operating spend.

Owner typically funds: Ramp marketing and loyalty enrollment while occupancy and rate build; recurring fees scale up as revenue mix stabilizes.

Brand typically provides: Negotiated ramp relief or co-op when offered, plus channel and mix guidance as the asset proves out.

Owner typically funds: Recurring program fees, reserves, and periodic standards-driven capex—moderate and predictable once stabilized.

Brand typically provides: Ongoing QA, brand campaigns, and systems access that justify the recurring fee stack.

Owner typically funds: Renewal or conversion PIP, owner reserves, and re-licensing work when triggers hit—not part of steady-state operations.

Brand typically provides: Clear renewal standards; co-investment or phased PIP timing may be negotiable in competitive renewals.

rows.title: To Join
rows.body: Application and entry fees; training and opening support; initial / franchise license fee; technology implementation / setup; plan review, design, or inspection fees. Basis and timing vary by keys, market, and deal—confirm in the FDD for your deal.

rows.title: To Operate
rows.body: Royalty or brand fee, marketing or brand fund, technology and systems, loyalty program participation, and reservation or distribution services—the recurring stack owners model every year. Understand what each line pays for and what is mandatory versus optional add-ons.

rows.title: When Things Change
rows.body: Renewal or conversion PIP, termination or liquidated damages themes, and owner-funded reserves when standards or performance events trigger capital. These items often surprise owners who only modeled the opening fee stack.

rows.title: Application & Feasibility
rows.body: Align asset profile, market, and conversion scope with brand development before LOI economics harden.

rows.title: Design & standards
rows.body: Kit-of-parts and QA review; owners plan capex and timeline around approved design milestones.

rows.title: Pre-Opening Planning
rows.body: Staffing, OS&E, systems implementation, and operator onboarding—cash burn often peaks here.

rows.title: Opening Support
rows.body: Training, soft opening, and QA readiness with heightened brand touchpoints.

rows.title: Stabilization
rows.body: Reporting cadence and commercial support shift from opening-weighted to steady-state rhythm.

rows.title: Term & renewal
rows.body: Expect a long initial franchise term with renewal options subject to notice, conditions, and brand standards compliance. Renewal may trigger property improvement expectations—confirm duration, notice party, and conditions in the agreement.

rows.title: Performance & exit
rows.body: Performance tests and QA programs are common—understand cure periods and who may terminate after failure. Early exit without cause may be limited; termination fees may apply. Confirm audit rights and caps on reimbursable expenses with counsel.

rows.title: Transfer & sale
rows.body: Assignment, change-of-control, and buyout provisions affect liquidity. Plan for brand approval paths before assuming a sale is frictionless. Area-of-protection themes define same-brand competition near your site—confirm exact geography in legal documents.
